info.bio:
Mickey & Sylvia was an R&B duo composed of Mickey "Guitar" Baker and Sylvia Van der Pool Robinson. They were the first big seller for Groove Records.

Mickey "Guitar" Baker was a music instructor, and Sylvia Robinson was one of his pupils. His guitar stylings, especially the insane soloing on "Love Is Strange", inspired a plethora of guitarists, including Sterling Morrison of the Velvet Underground.

Mickey & Sylvia had a hit with "Love Is Strange" in 1957.

scenes.name: Sugar Hill Records y Rapper’s Delight
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Sylvia Robinson, la «madre del hip hop», venía del R&B: Little Sylvia, el dúo Mickey & Sylvia («Love Is Strange», 1956), la producción del «It’s Gonna Work Out Fine» de Ike & Tina, el sello All Platinum con su marido Joe (con supuestos lazos mafiosos) y su propio éxito «Pillow Talk» (1973). Arruinada, vio a Lovebug Starski en Harlem World en 1979 y quiso grabar aquello; con Morris Levy fundaron Sugar Hill. Su hijo la llevó a una pizzería de Nueva Jersey donde Big Bank Hank, mánager de los Cold Crush, hizo una audición en su coche junto a Master Gee y Wonder Mike: la Sugarhill Gang. Sobre una recreación de «Good Times» de Chic grabaron quince minutos de rimas que una radio de St. Louis, WESL, se atrevió a poner: «Rapper’s Delight» inundó el mundo en otoño de 1979, dejó en anécdota el «King Tim III» de Fatback y demostró que el hip hop era negocio. En el Bronx sonaba a imitación higienizada: Hank rapeaba las rimas de Grandmaster Caz («I’m the C-A-S-AN, the O-V-A»), un estribillo de Hollywood y una frase de Rahiem; «hizo retroceder el hip hop cinco años» (Charlie Chase). Para Kool Moe Dee, sin Sugar Hill quizá no habría industria. La casa no pagaba bien a sus artistas, y su banda (Skip Alexander, Doug Wimbish, Duke Bootee) tocaba los temas. En Harlem, Bobby Robinson y su sello Enjoy ficharon a Flash, los Funky 4 + 1 y los Treacherous Three.

podcast.title: "Love Is Strange" Origin Story
podcast.body: The song originated from Bo Diddley, who had written and recorded it in May 1956 but not released it. Jody Williams, Bo Diddley's guitarist, played the song for Sylvia, who liked it, leading Mickey and Sylvia to record it and make it a hit. "But at that point, fate intervened in the form of Bo Deadly."

podcast.title: Diminishing Commercial Returns
podcast.body: While they released many more records after "Love Is Strange," their sales and chart performance steadily declined. Their next record went Top 10 R&B but only Pop #47, and the one after that, "Dearest," only reached #85 on the Hot 100. "Mickey and Sylvia would release many more records, but they would have diminishing returns."

podcast.title: End of Duo and Mickey's Departure
podcast.body: Their own recordings continued to be unsuccessful, and Mickey faced personal challenges due to his white wife amidst virulent racism in the US, alongside his increasing interest in academic music. These factors led him to move to Europe and pursue jazz and composition, effectively ending the duo's active career. "However, Mickey and Sylvia's recordings under their own name were still having no success, and Mickey was also having problems because his then wife was white, and with the particularly virulent form of racism the US was suffering through at the time, he didn't want to be in the country anymore."

podcast.title: Formation as a Duo
podcast.body: The duo was formed when Sylvia started taking guitar lessons from Mickey Baker. Different sources attribute the idea to either Joe Robinson (inspired by Jean and Junis) or Mickey Baker (who wanted to emulate Les Paul and Mary Ford). The gimmick was a male-female duo who could both sing and play guitar, focusing on Mickey's string-bending style. "Eventually it was decided that Sylvia should join with her guitar teacher and former duo."

podcast.title: Independent Venture: Willow Records
podcast.body: After being dropped from Vic Records, Mickey and Sylvia temporarily split but later reunited to form their own company, Willow Records, to release their material independently. "After Mickey and Sylvia were dropped along with the rest of the Vic artists. This bled up temporarily, but then got back together to start their own company, Willow Records, to release their own material."

podcast.title: Informing of Rudy Lewis's Death
podcast.body: Sylvia Van Topoe of Mickey and Sylvia was the person who informed Johnny Moore of The Drifters about the sudden death of Rudy Lewis on May 21, 1964. "Johnny Moore bumped into Sylvia Van Topoe of Mickey and Sylvia, and she said, thank God it wasn't you."

podcast.title: Move to Groove Records (RCA Subsidiary)
podcast.body: Their airplay in New York attracted the attention of Bob Rollant at Groove Records, a subsidiary of RCA established in 1953 as a "fake indie label" to access the R&B market. "But the records did get some airplay in New York, if nowhere else, and that brought them to the attention of Bob Rullant's at Groove Records."

podcast.title: Onstage Chemistry, Offstage Discord
podcast.body: Mickey and Sylvia had musical chemistry on stage and recordings, but offstage, they soon began to "great on each other" due to their contrasting personalities and ambitions. "But they worked well as a musical team, even if they were never going to be the best of friends."

podcast.title: Post-Hit Decline and RCA Label Closure
podcast.body: After "Love Is Strange" became a breakthrough hit, RCA controversially closed Groove Records and moved its artists and producer Valence to another subsidiary, Vic Records. This loss of momentum severely affected Mickey and Sylvia's career, leading to diminishing returns on subsequent releases. "But after groove records that had this breakthrough big hit, RCA decided to close the label down and move the acts on the label and their producer Valence to another subsidiary. Vic."

podcast.title: Production for Ike & Tina Turner
podcast.body: To return a favor for Ike Turner playing on some of their Willow Records, Mickey and Sylvia agreed to produce a record for Ike & Tina Turner. They suggested "It's Gonna Work Out Fine," a song they had previously recorded for Vic (unreleased), and handled its production and arrangement, with Sylvia playing lead guitar and Mickey providing spoken vocals. "Ag Turner played on some of their records, and to return the favour they agreed to produce a record for Ag and Tina Turner."

podcast.title: Rainbow Records Signing
podcast.body: Their first label was Rainbow Records, a medium-sized indie label in New York. Their initial singles, "I'm So Glad" and "Se De Boom Run Dun," did not sell well, but gained some airplay in New York, attracting attention from larger labels. "Originally, they signed with the label called Rainbow Records, a medium-sized indie label in New York, where they put out their first single, I'm so glad."

podcast.title: Recording Team at Groove Records
podcast.body: At Groove Records, Mickey and Sylvia were paired with saxophonist and arranger King Curtis, whom Mickey already knew from Doc Pomus. Curtis assembled a team of top R&B musicians in New York, many of whom also played on Atlantic sessions. "Valence put them together with the sex-offenist and arranger King Curtis, who Mickey already knew from his work with Doc Pommas, and Curtis put together a team of the best R&B musicians in New York, many of them the same people who would play on most of Atlantic sessions."

podcast.title: Shirley and Lee Imitators
podcast.body: Mickey and Sylvia were noted as imitators of the New Orleans R&B duo Shirley and Lee, reflecting the influence of Shirley and Lee's sound on other artists. "spawned a host of emitators, including Jean and Eunice and Mickey and Sylvia."
